source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: A retrieval-augmented LM system with a fine-tuned reasoner and ensembling nears the human crowd aggregate but does not beat it on average.
numbers: Test set 914 questions after the June 2023 cutoff. System Brier .179 vs crowd .149 vs random .250. Dataset: 33,664 binary questions from 5 platforms, 2015-2024.
limits: Crowd is a strong baseline. Model hedges toward the middle. A later critique (c24) flags leakage risks in such backtests.
agent_relevance: Plain LM calls are far from crowd level; a scaffold of retrieve, reason, aggregate closes much of the gap.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: The system beats the crowd only when three conditions hold together: crowd unsure, early retrieval dates, at least 5 relevant articles.
numbers: With all three met the system beats the crowd by more than 1.5 standard errors in Brier and accuracy. When crowd said .3-.7, crowd Brier .24 vs system .237 (unweighted average with crowd).
limits: Condition subsets are small. Gains are tied to retrieval quality.
agent_relevance: Gate the agent: trust its own forecast when evidence is rich and the prior is uncertain, else defer to a base rate (fits G1: doubt only on a signal).

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Averaging the system with the crowd beats either alone, with the crowd weighted most.
numbers: Weighted average with 4x crowd weight (chosen on validation) moved Brier from .149 to .146 on the full test set.
limits: Needs a crowd to exist at forecast time.
agent_relevance: Combining unlike sources beats either; consistent with G4 (same-model agreement is weak, independent sources help).

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Among 5 ensembling rules (mean, median, geometric mean, trimmed mean, universal self-consistency variant) trimmed mean was best on validation. Ablations show small gaps.
numbers: Full system .179; fine-tuned GPT-3.5 swapped in .182; base GPT-4 without fine-tuned reasoner .181; base GPT-4 without retrieval .183 (all vs crowd .149; standard errors .002-.003).
limits: Gaps between ablation rows are near the standard errors.
agent_relevance: Pick the aggregation rule by code on held-out data (G5). Base-model strength mattered less than the pipeline.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Self-supervised fine-tuning on the model's own reasonings that beat the crowd improved forecasts.
numbers: 13,253 fine-tuning samples; fine-tuned GPT-3.5 reached .182 vs .179 for fine-tuned GPT-4.
limits: Training, not scaffold alone; prompt-only gains were small in the authors' search.
agent_relevance: Training-free analogue: keep reasoning patterns that were outcome-scored right, chosen by code, not by self-judgement.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy
finding: A crowd of 12 different LLMs matched a 925-person human tournament crowd on 31 binary questions (preregistered).
numbers: LLM crowd Brier M=.20 (SD .12) vs human crowd M=.19 (SD .19), t(60)=0.19, p=.850. Better than 0.25 baseline: t(30)=-2.35, p=.026. Best single model GPT-4 .15; Coral (Command) .38.
limits: Only 31 questions, low power (see c23). Equivalence only inside a medium effect bound (0.081).
agent_relevance: Many different models aggregated by code works for weak forecasters; G4 says use different models, not samples of one.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy
finding: LLM crowd shows an acquiescence bias: mean predictions above 50% although outcomes split almost evenly.
numbers: Mean model prediction 57.35% (SD 20.93), t(1006)=86.20, p<.001 against 50%.
limits: Pooled across model-question cells, which are not independent.
agent_relevance: Shared directional bias survives averaging; check calibration, do not extremize.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy
finding: Study 2: showing a model the median human forecast improved it, but simple averaging of human and machine was better still.
numbers: GPT-4 and Claude 2 improved 17% to 28% when given the human median as information; averaging human and machine forecasts was more accurate than the informed model.
limits: Exploratory, small question set.
agent_relevance: Combine in code rather than asking the model to integrate an outside number (G5).

source: Schoenegger and Park (2023) Large Language Model Prediction Capabilities: Evidence from a Real-World Forecasting Tournament
finding: Early test: GPT-4 in a live Metaculus tournament (Jul-Oct 2023, 843 participants) was not better than always saying 50%.
numbers: GPT-4 mean Brier .20 (SD .18) vs human crowd median .07 (SD .08), N=23 binary questions. GPT-4 vs 0.25: t(22)=-1.23, p=.23. Crowd vs 0.25: t(22)=-10.69, p<.001.
limits: One prompt, one model, 23 questions. Superseded by later systems.
agent_relevance: Baseline: an unscaffolded 2023 frontier LLM had no detectable skill over chance on open questions.

source: Schoenegger and Park (2023) Large Language Model Prediction Capabilities: Evidence from a Real-World Forecasting Tournament
finding: The hypothesis that GPT-4 just hugs 50% was not supported; a Bayesian model average of GPT-4 and crowd was worse than the crowd alone.
numbers: BMA weights .467 GPT-4 and .533 crowd gave Brier .13 (SD .09), vs crowd alone .07.
limits: Weights came from likelihoods, not held-out tuning.
agent_relevance: Adding a weak forecaster to a strong crowd can hurt; weight by measured skill.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Leakage-free benchmark of 1,000 unresolved questions: superforecasters beat the best LLM; the public median roughly tied it.
numbers: 200-question subset: superforecasters Brier .096 (39 people), general public .121 (p<.001 vs supers), top LLM Claude 3.5 Sonnet .122 (p<.001 vs supers).
limits: Absolute scores differ by question set (another view: supers .076, public .096).
agent_relevance: The gap to superforecasters is the live target. Use as a yardstick.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Prompt findings: scratchpad prompting was best; giving the human crowd forecast on market questions helped; news access did not help.
numbers: Best configurations mostly scratchpad plus crowd forecast input. Gap superforecasters vs GPT-4o 0.054 Brier, versus only 0.026 between GPT-4o and GPT-4.
limits: Prompt sweep limited (3 superforecaster-written prompts plus a few others).
agent_relevance: Structure and a strong prior input mattered more than raw added news text.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Skill scales with general model quality; a linear projection puts parity with superforecasters in the future.
numbers: Brier vs Chatbot Arena r=-0.68, p=0.003, R2=.47; parity near Arena 1406 (95% CI 1346-1633). Vs log compute r=-0.67, p=.046; parity near 6.49e26 FLOP (CI 9.69e25-8.65e28).
limits: Few points, wide intervals; compute fit only marginal.
agent_relevance: Scale helps, but scaffolds aim at the same gap now.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Public ForecastBench site lists a baseline track (no tools) and a tournament track (tools allowed) plus a linear-trend projection of LLM-superforecaster parity.
numbers: Homepage fetch gave no figures; leaderboard values not read this session.
limits: No numbers obtained; do not cite 2026 leaderboard values from this line.
agent_relevance: Re-check leaderboard before citing current figures.

source: Paleka et al. (2024) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: Logical-consistency checks (arbitrage metric) on related questions correlate with later Brier score, so quality can be estimated before outcomes resolve.
numbers: 2,621 resolved ground-truth questions in the benchmark; some checks (e.g. conditional probabilities) correlate R>0.9 with Brier, others little.
limits: Only some checks carry signal. Benchmark with 3,000 checks resolves in 2028.
agent_relevance: Code-run consistency checks (negation, conditional) are a cheap non-self-graded signal for G2/G3-style gating.

source: Paleka et al. (2024) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: ArbitrageForecaster, which patches a forecaster by arbitraging related questions, improved the checks it targeted but not held-out checks and not real accuracy.
numbers: Authors report consistency gains on optimized checks do not generalize to held-out checks and do not improve Brier.
limits: Negative result; small model set.
agent_relevance: Forcing consistency alone is not accuracy; fits G3 (pass on something not fitted to).

source: Hsieh, Fu, Chen (2024) Reasoning and Tools for Human-Level Forecasting
finding: ReAct agents with retrieval and a Python simulation tool, ensembled, matched the crowd; plain base LMs did not.
numbers: RTF median of 3 Brier .169 (acc 72.4%), mean of 3 .170 (73.9%) vs crowd .172 (73.8%); Halawi et al. GPT-4o .177; plain GPT-4o .210; GPT-4 .265, GPT-3.5 .261, Llama 3 .256 (worse than 0.25).
limits: Small question set; ensemble sizes 3-4; reported as a workshop-style result.
agent_relevance: Tools plus an agent loop is the method already used in LLM agent loops; ensembles helped agents (.169 vs .180 sampled) but not base LMs (.218 vs .210).

source: Hsieh, Fu, Chen (2024) Reasoning and Tools for Human-Level Forecasting
finding: ReAct agent ensembles had lower spread and better calibration than base-LM ensembles.
numbers: Ensemble standard deviation .092 (ReAct, size 3) vs .150 (base LMs, size 4). Calibration index .0129 (ReAct mean) vs .0194 (GPT-4o).
limits: Single question set; calibration index definition author-specific.
agent_relevance: Lower variance between runs signals evidence-grounding; run-to-run spread is a usable code-side uncertainty signal.

source: Pratt et al. (2024) Can Language Models Use Forecasting Strategies?
finding: Superforecaster-style strategies in prompts (decomposition, base rates, personas, news) all made GPT-4-class forecasts worse than one plain prompt.
numbers: The plain single prompt beat the human prediction-market baseline on Brier; every added strategy scored worse. Weighted Brier showed models guess low probability, so Resolve-Yes events scored far worse than Resolve-No.
limits: Dataset skewed to events that mostly do not occur, which flatters low guesses; one base model.
agent_relevance: Do not bolt on human superforecasting recipes by default (G1: doubt only on a signal). Measure on both outcome classes.

source: Pratt et al. (2024) Can Language Models Use Forecasting Strategies?
finding: The authors argue models mostly predict that events are unlikely, which can look like skill when most questions resolve No.
numbers: Weighted Brier separates events that resolved positively from those that resolved negatively; Yes-resolved Brier was much higher than No-resolved for every method.
limits: Their follow-up explanation; not independently replicated here.
agent_relevance: Always report Brier split by outcome; a base-rate trick can pass a plain Brier test.

source: Zou et al. (2022) Forecasting Future World Events with Neural Networks (Autocast)
finding: Early dataset: language models were far below the human crowd; retrieval from a dated news corpus and model size helped.
numbers: Largest static FiD model had 40% calibration error vs 8% for the human crowd; using crowd forecasts as input (temporal FiD) cut it to 17%. Reported relative gains over UnifiedQA-v2 and T5 baselines: 93% and 15% (average score).
limits: 2022-era models; older benchmark.
agent_relevance: Origin of the retrieve-by-date design reused by later systems; shows calibration, not just accuracy, was the early gap.

source: Turtel et al. (2025) Outcome-based Reinforcement Learning to Predict the Future
finding: A 14B reasoning model trained with outcome-based RL on Brier loss matched or beat o1 on Polymarket questions and calibrated better.
numbers: 1,265 held-out questions. 7-run ReMax ensemble Brier .190 [.178,.203], ECE .062; o1 about .201 (implied by the -.011 difference); base DeepSeek-R1 14B .215, ECE .089. Simulated one-share bets: profit $52 vs $39 for o1. Median-prediction sampling at inference helped.
limits: Trained, not scaffold; market price remained better (+.039 Brier vs market, per table).
agent_relevance: Median of several samples is the aggregation rule; per-question std scaling hurt calibration in RL, so keep Brier-proportional signals.

source: Hambly et al. (2025) Bench To The Future: A Pastcasting Benchmark for Forecasting Agents
finding: Offline 'pastcasting' with a fixed web corpus gives results comparable to live forecasting and tracks model progress; agents beat no-evidence prompts.
numbers: Brier: Claude Sonnet 3.5 (orig) .1925, 3.5 v2 .1690, 3.7 .1712, 3.7 thinking .1645, Sonnet 4 .1560, Sonnet 4 thinking .1597, Gemini 2.5 Pro .1611. Sonnet 3.5 vs Sonnet 4 p=.0024; Sonnet 4 vs thinking p=.53. No-evidence forecasters still beat 0.25.
limits: Absolute Brier hard to interpret; hundreds of questions; ReAct agent beat fixed-evidence forecaster.
agent_relevance: Extended thinking gave no clear gain here; evidence gathering did. They also argue the 31-question silicon-crowd study lacked power.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Pitfalls in Evaluating Language Model Forecasters
finding: Reported LLM-forecaster gains may be inflated by temporal leakage, search date filters that fail, and benchmark gaming.
numbers: At least 3.8% of one dataset and at least 10% of another trivial to resolve by logic; one dataset over 90% shortcut-prone; weak classifiers reach over 80% on some question sets. Date-restricted search returned leaked results (e.g. 'jan 6' restricted before 2020).
limits: Position paper with examples, not a re-run of every system.
agent_relevance: Treat headline parity claims (c01, c06) cautiously; judge our agent only on unresolved or pastcast-with-hermetic-corpus questions.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Pitfalls in Evaluating Language Model Forecasters
finding: Scoring rules can reward gambling: committing to one outcome beats a calibrated strategy on a leaderboard half the time.
numbers: Worked example: 50% chance of topping the benchmark by betting on one election result, versus a calibrated strategy; Brier over-weights high base-rate questions; calibration can penalize useful forecasting.
limits: Conceptual argument, no measured rates.
agent_relevance: Use rank-free metrics and multiple seeds; do not optimize the agent to a single Brier number.

source: Schoenegger, Park, Karger, Trott, Tetlock (2024) AI-Augmented Predictions: LLM Assistants Improve Human Forecasting Accuracy
finding: Human forecasters (N=991) who consulted a GPT-4-Turbo assistant were 24-28% more accurate than control, even with a deliberately biased assistant.
numbers: 6 questions. Superforecasting-style assistant and noisy (overconfident, base-rate-neglecting) assistant both improved accuracy 24-28% vs control. Excluding one outlier item: 41% vs 29%. Preregistered; Cohen d=0.20 power analysis.
limits: Control got a weaker model, so gains partly reflect any strong LLM; one outlier question drove variance; 6 questions only.
agent_relevance: Humans gain from a model that gives numbers and arguments; the noisy assistant also helped, so effect is not proof the advice was correct.

source: Lu (2025) Evaluating LLMs on Real-World Forecasting Against Expert Forecasters
finding: By mid-2025, reasoning models beat the Halawi-era crowd benchmark but remain far from paid expert forecasters on Metaculus.
numbers: 464 Metaculus questions. o3 Brier .1352, o3-pro .1386, GPT-4.1 .1542, o4-mini .1589, DeepSeek-v3 .1798, Claude 3.6 Sonnet .1810, GPT-4o .1883, DeepSeek-r1 .1950, Qwen3-32B .2066, GPT-4o-mini .2743. Experts (152-question subset) about .023 vs o3 .135. Hold-out o3-pro .1307.
limits: Experts predicted only 31-47% of questions, so subsets differ; absolute Brier not comparable across question sets; Brier averaged over 5 predictions per model.
agent_relevance: About 0.14 Brier vs 0.19 a year earlier: forecasting skill rises quickly with reasoning models, but a large expert gap remains.

source: Lu (2025) Evaluating LLMs on Real-World Forecasting Against Expert Forecasters
finding: Prompting as a story ('narrative prediction') made all models worse than asking directly; models forecast politics better than economics.
numbers: Narrative Brier: Qwen3-32B .2218, Claude 3.6 Sonnet .2267, DeepSeek-v3 .2633, GPT-4o-mini .2942 (mean ensembles); direct prompts better for every model listed. Models did better on politics than on economics and finance.
limits: Single prompt contrast; category cells have under 30 questions.
agent_relevance: Direct, plain probability elicitation beats fiction framing; keep elicitation format fixed and simple.
